D. Damp litmus loses its colour [1]

(11) Which test/result pair is correct for hydrogen?
A. Glowing splint relights
B. Lighted splint: squeaky pop
C. Damp red litmus turns blue
D. Limewater becomes milky [1]

(12) Which test/result pair is correct for oxygen?
A. A glowing splint relights
B. Clear limewater turns milky
C. A lighted splint pops
D. Damp litmus loses colour [1]

(1) C. Red. Lithium gives a red flame.
Distractor explanations: A: Lilac is the potassium flame colour. B: Green is the barium flame colour. D: Bright yellow indicates sodium.

(2) B. It detects contamination on the wire. A blank distinguishes carry-over from sample evidence.
Distractor explanations: A: A blank contains no sample and cannot establish its colour. C: A blank flame is not a quantitative concentration measurement. D: Checking the wire does not prove sample purity.

(3) C. Bright sodium emission masks other colours. A strong yellow observation can mask weaker colours.
Distractor explanations: A: Masking is an optical effect, not chemical removal of the other ion. B: Different ions retain different emissions in mixtures. D: The other salt need not become colourless; its emission is obscured.

(4) D. Lilac. Potassium gives lilac.
Distractor explanations: A: Bright yellow indicates sodium. B: Brick-red indicates calcium. C: Green indicates barium.

(5) C. Brick-red. Calcium gives brick-red.
Distractor explanations: A: Lilac indicates potassium. B: Bright yellow indicates sodium. D: Red is the lithium flame colour, not the calcium colour.

(6) A. Green. Barium gives green.
Distractor explanations: B: Bright yellow indicates sodium. C: Red indicates lithium in these tests. D: Lilac indicates potassium.

(7) B. Dissolved ammonia creates the alkaline conditions. The damp indicator responds to the aqueous alkaline condition.
Distractor explanations: A: Water alone does not create the alkaline response. C: Ammonia dissolves in the moisture rather than merely displacing it. D: Dampness does not convert nitrogen gas into ammonia.

(8) D. It turns blue. Ammonia gives an alkaline response.
Distractor explanations: A: Ammonia makes damp red litmus alkaline, so it does change colour. B: Bleaching is the chlorine response, not ammonia’s. C: The expected alkaline endpoint is blue, not permanently purple.

(9) A. Insoluble calcium carbonate forms a precipitate. A precipitate scatters light in the liquid.
Distractor explanations: B: Calcium hydrogen carbonate is soluble and does not cause the milkiness. C: Carbon dioxide reacts in solution rather than depositing as white solid CO2. D: The test does not reduce calcium ions to calcium metal.

(10) D. Damp litmus loses its colour. Chlorine removes the litmus colour.
Distractor explanations: A: This is the ammonia response. B: This is the hydrogen test. C: This is the oxygen test.

(11) B. Lighted splint: squeaky pop. Hydrogen uses a lighted splint and pop.
Distractor explanations: A: This is the oxygen test. C: This is the ammonia test. D: This is the carbon dioxide test.

(12) A. A glowing splint relights. Oxygen supports renewed burning of the glowing splint.
Distractor explanations: B: This is the carbon dioxide test. C: This is the hydrogen test. D: This is the chlorine test.

items.prompt:
(a) State the effect of ammonia on damp red litmus. [1]

(b) Describe how limewater is used to test for carbon dioxide and give the positive observation. [2]

(c) Explain why a glowing splint relights in oxygen. [2]

(d) Suggest a method and reason for checking a suspected potassium flame result that appears mainly yellow with a faint lilac component. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) It turns blue.

(b) Bubble a small gas sample through clear limewater; it becomes milky if carbon dioxide is present.

(c) Oxygen supports combustion, so the glowing splint starts burning with a flame again.

(d) Clean the wire, check its blank flame and repeat the test. This removes possible sodium carry-over so a persistent lilac potassium colour can be distinguished from yellow contamination.
marking_guidance: Part a: Blue (1).
Part b: Gas through limewater (1).
Part b: Milky/cloudy observation (1).
Part c: Glowing splint relights (1).
Part c: Oxygen supports combustion (1).
Part d: Clean/check blank/repeat (1).
Part d: Distinguish sodium yellow contamination from lilac potassium (1).

items.prompt:
A solution X contains one of Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺ and one of Cl⁻, Br⁻ or I⁻. The following laboratory record applies to all five parts.

| Portion | Treatment | Observation |
|---|---|---|
| A | NaOH added dropwise | Light-blue solid appears |
| A | More NaOH added until in excess | The solid remains |
| B | Aqueous ammonia added dropwise, then in excess | Light-blue solid first appears; in excess it disappears and the liquid is deep blue |
| C | Reserved, untreated portion | Available for a halide test |

A subsequent test on C produces a white silver-salt precipitate. No repeat trials or purity measurements have been made.

(a) Complete the table for portion A.

| Feature | Result |
|---|---|
| Initial appearance after adding NaOH | ______ |
| Behaviour after adding excess NaOH | ______ |
| Physical state of the coloured material | ______ | [3]

(b) Deduce the cation from A and B, and correct the description “deep-blue precipitate in excess ammonia” using the recorded change in B. [2]

(c) Describe the reagent sequence to carry out the halide test on the reserved portion C before obtaining the recorded white precipitate. [2]

(d) Explain the anion identification supported by the result from (c), why nitric acid is used instead of hydrochloric acid, and why portion C was kept separate from A. [3]

(e) Explain why the tests do not establish that X contains only the ions you identified, and give one improvement to the strength of the identification evidence. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Initially a light-blue precipitate forms. In excess NaOH it remains as an insoluble solid, rather than becoming a blue solution.

(b) Cu²⁺ is supported. In excess ammonia the solid disappears, so the deep-blue material is a solution, not a precipitate.

(c) Add dilute nitric acid to C, followed by aqueous silver nitrate.

(d) The white silver precipitate supports chloride. Hydrochloric acid would introduce chloride and could create the positive result itself. Separate C avoids NaOH carried over from A interfering with the silver-nitrate test.

(e) Positive tests support the presence of the named ions, not the absence of every other substance. Repeat the tests on fresh portions with appropriate controls, or use a further independent identification test.
marking_guidance: Part a: Initial light-blue precipitate recorded (1).
Part a: Solid remains in excess, so it is insoluble (1).
Part a: Physical state correctly identified as a solid/precipitate, not a solution (1).
Part b: Cu²⁺ / copper(II) (1).
Part b: Deep-blue solution because the solid has dissolved; the label precipitate is incorrect (1).
Part c: Acidify the fresh portion with dilute nitric acid (1).
Part c: Then add aqueous silver nitrate (1).
Part d: Chloride / Cl⁻ from the white silver precipitate (1).
Part d: HCl introduces chloride, so it could cause a false positive (1).
Part d: A separate portion avoids carry-over of NaOH/earlier reagents into this test (1).
Part e: Presence of the ions does not exclude other dissolved substances/purity is not established (1).
Part e: Repeat on fresh portions with appropriate controls or use an independent confirmatory test (1).
